af-1.title: What AI Fluency actually means
af-1.why: Most people treat AI as a magic box — you put a question in, hope for a useful answer. AI Fluency is the opposite: a systematic approach to collaboration that makes outcomes predictable and useful.
instructions: AI Fluency ≠ prompt engineering tricks. It's the ability to work with AI as a skilled collaborator — knowing when to use it, how to guide it, and when to step back.
Think of it like language fluency. You don't need to know grammar rules to hold a conversation — but you do need enough internalized structure to communicate precisely. Same with Claude.

Three levels of AI use: Occasional user (one-off prompts, unpredictable results) → Competent user (clear prompts, knows limitations) → Fluent collaborator (integrates AI into workflow, calibrates based on task type).
This course moves you from level 1 toward level 3. Not by learning tricks — by building a durable mental model.
af-1.validate: You can explain in one sentence what separates an AI-fluent user from someone who just types questions into Claude.
af-1.tip: The single most valuable AI Fluency skill: knowing when NOT to use AI. A 20-second mental check before each task saves more time than any prompt technique.

af-2.title: How Claude actually processes your requests
af-2.why: Claude is not a search engine, not a database, and not a thinking entity. Understanding what it actually does explains both its remarkable capabilities and its predictable failure modes.
instructions: Claude is a large language model. At its core, it predicts what text should come next based on patterns learned from massive amounts of training data. This sounds simple — the results are surprisingly powerful.

What this means in practice: Claude is excellent at tasks involving language patterns — analysis, synthesis, drafting, explaining, restructuring, coding. It's less reliable on tasks requiring precise recall of specific facts, real-time data, or strict logical chains.

The knowledge cutoff: Claude was trained on data up to a specific date. It doesn't know what happened after that unless you tell it or enable [[node:cap-search|web search]]. Asking about recent events without web search enabled is a common source of confident-sounding wrong answers.

Why it sometimes sounds confident and wrong: the model is optimized to be helpful and produce fluent text. Sometimes that means generating a plausible-sounding answer rather than saying 'I don't know.' This is called hallucination.
What you can do: treat Claude's output as a strong first draft from a very capable but imperfect collaborator. Verify specific facts that matter. Use web search for anything time-sensitive.
af-2.validate: You understand why Claude can write a brilliant analysis and simultaneously get a specific date or name wrong in the same response.
af-2.tip: A simple mental model: Claude is extremely good at reasoning about things, and unreliable about remembering specific things. Design your prompts accordingly — give it the facts, ask it to reason.

af-3.title: The 4D Collaboration Framework
af-3.why: Most AI interactions fail not because the model is bad, but because the collaboration design is weak. The 4D Framework gives you a repeatable structure that works across any task type.
instructions: The 4D Framework: Describe → Delegate → Discern → Develop. Each step is a question you ask before or during your interaction with Claude.

DESCRIBE: Give Claude enough context to do the task well. Who are you? What's the goal? What format do you need? What's the audience? Most prompts fail because they're missing this. Rule: a good description takes 30–60 seconds to write and saves 5–10 minutes of back-and-forth.

DELEGATE: Choose the right tasks for AI. Claude excels at: drafting, summarizing, explaining, restructuring, brainstorming, code. Claude is weak at: tasks requiring current information (without search), precise numerical calculations, tasks where being wrong has serious consequences. Delegation isn't about using AI for everything — it's about strategic choice.

DISCERN: Evaluate the output critically. Check: Does this answer the actual question? Are specific facts verifiable? Does the reasoning hold up? Does the output match the format I need? Never paste AI output directly into something important without reading it carefully.

DEVELOP: Improve based on what you learned. If Claude missed the mark — why? Was the description unclear? Was it the wrong task for AI? Adjust the prompt or your approach. Over time, you build a personal library of what works.
af-3.prompt:
Try this structure:

Role: [Who Claude should act as]
Context: [What this is about, who the audience is]
Task: [Exactly what you need]
Format: [How you want the output structured]
Constraints: [What to avoid or include]
af-3.validate: You can apply all four Ds to a real task you need to do today.
af-3.tip: You don't need to use this framework explicitly every time — after a few iterations it becomes automatic. But writing it out explicitly for the first few tasks dramatically accelerates the learning curve.

af-4.title: Ethics and responsible use
af-4.why: AI fluency includes knowing where the edges are — privacy, accuracy responsibility, and the human judgment that AI can't replace.
instructions: Privacy: think before you paste. [[node:pl-web-setup|Claude.ai]] has a privacy policy, but the safest approach is to not input confidential client data, personal health information, trade secrets, or anything you wouldn't want stored on a third-party server. If your organization has an enterprise agreement, the rules may be different — check.

Accuracy responsibility: when you use Claude's output, you own the result. If Claude gets a fact wrong and you publish it without checking, that's on you. AI fluency means always keeping human judgment in the loop for anything that matters.

Transparency: in professional contexts, it's increasingly expected to be clear about AI use. This doesn't mean flagging every email you drafted with AI help — it means being honest when AI substantially shaped important work.

Dependency trap: if you stop writing, analyzing, or thinking because Claude does it for you — you're degrading skills you'll need. Use AI to extend your capabilities, not replace your thinking. Ask: am I learning something from this interaction, or just outsourcing it?
af-4.validate: You have a personal policy for what you will and won't input into Claude, and when you'll disclose AI use.
af-4.tip: A practical privacy rule: ask yourself if you'd be comfortable if that data appeared in a training set somewhere. If not, rephrase it abstractly or leave it out.

af-5.title: Measuring value and building the habit
af-5.why: AI fluency isn't a state you reach — it's a practice you develop. Measuring whether it's actually helping you is what separates deliberate users from people who use AI out of habit.
instructions: Track time honestly: does Claude save you time, or does fixing its output take as long as doing it yourself? For tasks that consistently take longer to fix than write — stop delegating those tasks.

Quality signals to watch: Are your drafts improving as starting points? Are you getting to better answers faster? Are you exploring ideas you wouldn't have thought of alone? If yes — the habit is working.

When NOT to use Claude: tasks you do faster yourself; tasks where the thinking process IS the value (creative work you want to own fully); tasks where the stakes are high enough that you'd need to verify everything anyway; tasks where personal voice matters.
Build a simple habit: pick one recurring task (weekly report, meeting notes, research summaries) and commit to trying Claude's approach for 2 weeks. Measure time before and after. Then decide.
af-5.validate: You have identified at least one task to test and one metric to measure.
af-5.tip: The best AI users are not the ones who use AI the most. They're the ones who've figured out exactly which 20% of their work benefits enormously from AI and focus there.

af-6.title: Your learning path forward
af-6.why: AI Fluency is the foundation. What you build on it depends on your goals. This step maps your next moves in 105 Atlas.
instructions: If you use Claude for everyday tasks (writing, research, analysis): take 'Claude Basics', then 'Prompting Techniques', then 'Ready Prompts'. These give you practical tools for the most common use cases.
If you use Claude for business or [[node:p-team|team work]]: take 'Claude for Business' next. It covers team adoption, creating shared instructions, and measuring organizational ROI.
If you're an educator: take 'Claude for Educators' — it covers lesson planning, academic integrity policies, and student guidance without replacing thinking.
If you're a developer: take 'Claude Setup', then '[[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] 101'. The developer track covers API usage, automation, Claude Code, MCP integrations, and agent systems.

Regardless of your path: the three most impactful things you can do right now are (1) set up [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] in your Claude account, (2) create a Project for your main area of work, (3) try one real task using the 4D Framework today.

claude-project-architecture.whatItIs: A hands-on course where you build a real, working Claude project structure from scratch — by the end, you have a personalized workspace where Claude remembers your context, follows your preferences, and runs your recurring tasks without re-explaining everything each time. applyIn.title: Any recurring work you do with Claude
applyIn.description: Once built, your architecture means you open Claude and it already knows who you are, what you're working on, and how you like things done. No more re-explaining.

applyIn.title: Multi-project organization
applyIn.description: Once you build one architecture, you have a template. Creating a second project for a new area of work takes 15 minutes instead of 3 weeks.

pitfalls: Making Project Instructions too long — Claude reads everything every time. Under 500 words is a good target for the first version.
Adding everything to Knowledge — too much context dilutes what Claude pays attention to. Be selective.
Trying to make it perfect before using it — start simple, use it for one week, then improve based on what's missing.

exercises.question: Open a chat without using your Project and ask Claude something you'd normally ask. Then open your Project and ask the same question. Compare the responses. What changed?
exercises.hint: The difference reveals exactly what your Project Instructions are doing for you.

exercises.hint: The best project architectures are built incrementally. Each thing you add should solve a specific friction you actually feel.

cpa-1.title: Why Claude needs architecture
cpa-1.why: Claude starts fresh every conversation. Without architecture, you re-explain your context, preferences, and goals every single time. With architecture, Claude arrives pre-briefed — ready to work at full quality from message one.
instructions: The core problem: Claude has no persistent memory by default. Each conversation is a blank slate. You lose context, quality drops, and you repeat yourself constantly.

The solution: a Project with architecture. A Project gives Claude permanent context — instructions it reads every session, knowledge it can reference, and templates that standardize how recurring tasks are done.

Three layers of a Claude project architecture:
  1. Project Instructions — what Claude always knows (your identity, goals, style, constraints)
  2. Project Knowledge — reference documents Claude can search (your materials, templates, data)
  3. Skills (Prompt Templates) — saved instructions for recurring tasks (your workflows, reviews, drafts)

The mental model: think of your Project as hiring a new Claude team member. Project Instructions = their onboarding document. Knowledge = the reference library you give them. Skills = the SOPs they follow for recurring tasks.
What you'll build: by step 6, you'll have all three layers working for a real area of your work.
cpa-1.validate: You understand why a blank-slate Claude is less useful than an architected one, and you know the three layers you'll build.
cpa-1.tip: The most valuable insight: architecture is not about making Claude smarter — it's about not wasting Claude's (and your) time on context you've already explained.

cpa-2.title: Create your Project workspace
cpa-2.why: Your Project is the container. Everything else lives inside it. Setting it up correctly takes 3 minutes and determines whether Claude always has the right context loaded.
instructions: Go to claude.ai → click 'Projects' in the left sidebar → '+ New project'.

Name your project specifically. Not 'My Project' — something like 'Marketing — Q3 Campaigns' or 'Content — Blog & Newsletter' or 'Research — Competitor Analysis'. The name is just for your navigation.
Add a brief description (1–2 sentences). Claude doesn't read this — it's for you when you have multiple projects.
You now have an empty project. Don't add anything yet — we'll add content step by step.
cpa-2.prompt:
Use this prompt to choose your project name:

I'm setting up a Claude Project workspace. Help me choose a good name.

My main area of work: [DESCRIBE YOUR WORK IN 1 SENTENCE]
The types of tasks I do most often: [LIST 3 TASKS]
How many different work areas I have: [NUMBER]

Suggest 3 specific project names that would help me stay organized. For each, explain what it would contain.
cpa-2.validate: You have a named, empty Claude Project ready to fill.
cpa-2.tip: Start with ONE project for your most active area of work. You can always create more. Trying to architect everything at once leads to analysis paralysis.

cpa-3.title: Write your Project Instructions (your Claude brief)
cpa-3.why: Project Instructions are what Claude reads before every single conversation in your project. This is the most important piece of your architecture. Good instructions mean Claude arrives fully briefed — bad instructions mean you're still re-explaining.
instructions: In your Project, click 'Edit project details' → 'Project instructions' → add your instructions here.

What good Project Instructions include:
  • WHO YOU ARE: your role, your organization, relevant background
  • WHAT THIS PROJECT IS FOR: the purpose, the goals, what success looks like
  • YOUR PREFERENCES: communication style, output format, level of detail
  • CONSTRAINTS: what to avoid, what you don't want Claude to do
  • CONTEXT: key facts Claude needs to know about your work
Length: aim for 200–400 words. Short enough that Claude actually uses all of it. Long enough to cover the key context.
Use the prompt below to have Claude WRITE your Project Instructions for you. Then paste the result into your project.
After pasting, test it: open a new conversation in your project and ask Claude something. Does the response reflect your instructions? If not, edit and improve.
cpa-3.prompt:
Copy this into a fresh Claude chat (not your project yet — we're drafting):

Help me write Project Instructions for my Claude workspace. I'll answer your questions, then you write the instructions.

Here's my context:
- My role/job: [YOUR ROLE]
- This project is for: [PROJECT PURPOSE]
- My main recurring tasks: [LIST 3–5 TASKS]
- My preferred response style: [FORMAL/CASUAL, SHORT/DETAILED, STRUCTURED/CONVERSATIONAL]
- Key things Claude should always know: [2–3 KEY FACTS]
- Things Claude should never do in this project: [YOUR CONSTRAINTS]

Write me Project Instructions in this format:
## About me
## This project's purpose
## How I want you to respond
## Key context
## What to avoid

Keep it under 350 words. Make it feel like a briefing document, not a list of rules.
cpa-3.validate: Your Project Instructions are pasted and saved. You've tested them with at least one conversation.
cpa-3.tip: The best Project Instructions are written over time, not all at once. After using your project for a week, you'll know exactly what was missing. Build the first version now; refine next week.

cpa-4.title: Add your Knowledge (what Claude can reference)
cpa-4.why: Project Knowledge is Claude's reference library. Unlike instructions (which Claude reads every time), Knowledge is searched when relevant. This is where your reference materials live — but only the ones Claude actually needs.
instructions: In your Project → 'Add content' → 'Add files' or paste text directly.

What belongs in Knowledge:
  ✓ Style guides, tone references, brand documents
  ✓ Process documentation, SOPs, checklists
  ✓ Templates you want Claude to follow
  ✓ Key reference data (product info, org charts, client profiles)
  ✓ Past examples of work you want Claude to match

What does NOT belong in Knowledge:
  ✗ General information Claude already knows (company history, public info)
  ✗ Sensitive data you don't want stored
  ✗ Outdated documents (they confuse more than help)
  ✗ Documents Claude will never need to reference
Quality rule: when in doubt, leave it out. 3 highly relevant documents beat 30 loosely relevant ones.
Use the prompt below to identify what to add to YOUR project's knowledge base.
cpa-4.prompt:
Paste this into your project (after you've set up instructions):

Help me decide what to add to my project's knowledge base.

My project is for: [YOUR PROJECT PURPOSE]
Documents I could potentially add: [LIST YOUR AVAILABLE DOCUMENTS]

For each document I listed, tell me:
1. Should I add it? (Yes / No / Maybe)
2. Why or why not
3. If yes — what specifically should Claude use it for?

Also suggest what types of documents I should CREATE to add, if I don't have them yet.
cpa-4.validate: You have 2–5 relevant documents in your Knowledge base. You know why each one is there.
cpa-4.tip: Add a 'Working Examples' document: past outputs that represent your best work. Tell Claude: 'Match the style and quality of these examples.' This immediately improves output quality.

cpa-5.title: Build your first Skill (a reusable template)
cpa-5.why: A Skill is a saved prompt template for a task you do repeatedly. Instead of explaining how to write a weekly report every week, you save the instructions once and reuse them. Your first Skill will immediately save you time.
instructions: A Skill isn't code — it's a saved, reusable instruction that you can call on whenever you need it. Think of it as a recipe card for Claude.
Choose your first Skill: pick the single task you do most often with Claude. Examples: 'Write my weekly summary', 'Review this document', 'Brainstorm ideas for X', 'Draft a response to this email'.

Anatomy of a good Skill prompt:
  • ROLE: who Claude is acting as
  • CONTEXT: what this task is about
  • INPUT: what you'll provide
  • TASK: exactly what you want done
  • FORMAT: how to structure the output
  • CONSTRAINTS: what to avoid

Save your Skill in one of two ways:
  a) Add it to your Project Knowledge as 'skill-[name].md'
  b) Keep it in a separate document on your computer to paste when needed
Use the prompt below to have Claude write your first Skill template for you.
cpa-5.prompt:
Paste this into your project:

Help me create a reusable Skill template for a task I do regularly.

The task: [DESCRIBE YOUR RECURRING TASK]
How often I do it: [FREQUENCY]
What I usually provide as input: [WHAT YOU GIVE CLAUDE]
What output I need: [WHAT YOU WANT BACK]
Format I prefer: [HOW IT SHOULD BE STRUCTURED]
Quality I'm aiming for: [DESCRIBE A GOOD RESULT]

Write me a complete Skill template I can save and reuse. Include:
- A title for the Skill
- The full prompt I should use each time (with [PLACEHOLDER] for things I'll fill in)
- Instructions for how to use it
- One example input and output to calibrate quality
cpa-5.validate: You have a saved Skill template for your most common task. You've tested it once with real input.
cpa-5.tip: The test for a good Skill: could you give this template to a colleague and they'd get the same quality output as you? If yes, it's well-written. If not, it's still too vague.

cpa-6.title: Run your first complete workflow
cpa-6.why: Having architecture that works is the goal — not having architecture that exists. This step runs a real task through your full system: Project context + Instructions + Knowledge + Skill. You'll see the difference.
instructions: Open your Project. You now have: Instructions (loaded automatically), Knowledge (available to reference), and a Skill template (ready to use).
Pick a real task you need to do this week. Open your Project, start a new conversation.
Notice: you don't need to explain who you are or what this project is about. Claude already knows.

Use your Skill template: paste it into the conversation with the actual input filled in. Watch Claude use the context from your Instructions and Knowledge to produce a better, more personalized result.
After the task, ask yourself: what would I have had to explain if I didn't have this project? That's your architecture's value.

Your architecture is now live. To improve it: whenever you find yourself explaining something Claude should already know, add it to Instructions. Whenever you do a task Claude should already know how to handle, save it as a Skill.
cpa-6.prompt:
Paste this into your project to review and improve your architecture after first use:

I just completed a task using our project. Help me improve the architecture.

The task I did: [DESCRIBE WHAT YOU DID]
Things I had to explain that Claude should have known: [LIST ANYTHING YOU HAD TO CLARIFY]
Things that worked well: [WHAT DIDN'T NEED EXPLANATION]
Output quality: [BETTER/SAME/WORSE than without the project?]

Based on this, suggest:
1. What to add or change in our Project Instructions
2. What new Skill to create next
3. What to add to Knowledge

Keep the suggestions specific and actionable.
cpa-6.validate: You've run a real task through your project architecture. You know what to improve for next week.
cpa-6.tip: Your project architecture is never 'done' — it grows with your usage. The best maintainers review and update it for 10 minutes every Friday: what worked, what didn't, what to add. Small weekly improvements compound into a dramatically better system over months.

claude-project-architecture.trigger: You want to build a personalized workspace in Claude — not slap things together ad hoc.
inputs: Knowledge base assets (docs, brand book, templates)
outputs: Ready Project architecture: instructions + KB + prompts
Claude remembers your context without reminders
A template for extending to new tasks
claude-project-architecture.savings: ~1 hour/day on re-explaining context to Claude

workflow-automation.title: Building an AI Workflow
workflow-automation.subtitle: Projects + Skills + Scenarios into a single automated process
workflow-automation.whatItIs: A practical course on creating AI workflows without code — for any user who wants to turn scattered Claude interactions into a coherent system. You will learn how Projects serve as containers, Skills as reusable modules, and Scenarios as application patterns. By the end you will have built your first end-to-end workflow and documented it for your team.
workflow-automation.approach: The course is structured as a workshop: each step produces an artifact you create for a real task from your own work. Theory is minimal — every concept is immediately reinforced with practice. By the final step you will have a documented workflow ready to hand off to a colleague.
outcomes: Can analyse a task and extract the workflow pattern: input → process → output
Structure Projects as workspaces with persistent context
Write reusable Skills — modules for repeating operations
Build step chains where the output of one step becomes the input of the next
Validate intermediate results — do not rely on Claude blindly
Document a workflow so a colleague can run it without your explanations

applyIn.title: Analytics and reporting
applyIn.description: Turn the cycle 'gather data → analyse → write report' into a repeatable workflow. Every step is documented, quality is stable, the next report takes half the time.

applyIn.title: Content and communications
applyIn.description: Email series, multi-channel posts, regular briefings — a workflow lets you reuse voice and structure instead of reinventing them every time.

applyIn.title: Operational processes
applyIn.description: Onboarding, request processing, meeting prep — any repeatable process with AI can be documented as a workflow and handed to the team without quality loss.

pitfalls: Trying to automate the entire process at once — start with one concrete step, make sure it works reliably, then add the next.
Building a workflow for a task that changes every time — automation adds value only where there is enough repetition and a predictable input.
Skipping validate steps to save time — checking intermediate results takes 2 minutes and prevents cascading errors across the whole chain.

exercises.question: Take any repeating task from your week and map it as a chain: what is the input, what are the transformation steps, what is the final output. How many steps require Claude, and how many require your own judgement?
exercises.hint: Steps that require judgement are your checkpoints. That is exactly where the workflow should pause and wait for human review.

exercises.question: Write a SKILL.md for one repeating operation you do every week. Show it to a colleague and ask: could they run this skill without your help?
exercises.hint: If your colleague asks more than two questions, the skill is not described well enough. Add examples and clarify the input format.

wa-1.title: What is an AI workflow: Projects, Skills, Scenarios
wa-1.why: Without shared terminology it is easy to confuse Projects, Skills and Scenarios — and build chaotic interactions instead of a system.
instructions: An AI workflow is a sequence of steps where Claude does part of the work and a human reviews the result and passes control forward. It is not magic — it is a repeatable process with clear inputs and outputs.
Project — container and workspace. It holds instructions (what Claude knows by default), a knowledge base (documents and context) and interaction history. One Project = one work area or task.
Skill — a reusable module: a description of one specific operation with an instruction, input format, output format and example. A Skill can be run again and again — the result will be predictable.

Scenario — an application pattern: a description of a specific situation where the workflow is used. One Skill can be used in multiple Scenarios. For example, the 'summarisation' skill is used in the 'weekly briefing' scenario and the 'meeting preparation' scenario.
Mental model: Project = the office. Skills = work instructions on the desk. Scenarios = the specific tasks the employee solves every day using those instructions.
wa-1.tip: Do not try to formalise everything at once. Start by describing what you do now — then break it down into Projects, Skills and Scenarios.
wa-1.validate: You can name one task from your work and explain what its Project will be, which Skill is needed and in which Scenario it is executed.

wa-2.title: Anatomy of a good workflow: input → process → output
wa-2.why: A workflow without a clear input/output structure cannot be repeated, handed to a colleague or improved — it runs differently every time.
instructions: Let us break it down with an example: 'preparing an analytical report'. Input: raw data (table, export, set of facts) + the question the report must answer. Process: 3 Claude steps (structure → analyse → format). Output: a finished report draft in an agreed format.
Three questions for any workflow: (1) What must be provided to Claude for it to begin? (2) What steps must be taken and in what order? (3) What does a result that counts as 'done' look like?
Describing the input is the most important part. Undefined input = unpredictable result. A good input description covers: data format, volume, required fields, language and any constraints.
Intermediate outputs are the inputs for the next steps. For each step write down: what is being passed forward and in what format. This lets you find bottlenecks before you run anything.
The final output must have a completion criterion: not 'a good report', but 'a report with an executive summary of up to 200 words, 3–5 key findings and recommendations as bullet points'.
wa-2.tip: Write the workflow on paper before opening Claude. Two hours on a diagram saves eight hours of iteration.
wa-2.validate: For your chosen task you have a description of the input, a list of steps and a completion criterion for the final output.

wa-3.title: Skills: creating your first reusable module
wa-3.why: Without a formalised Skill you reformulate the same task every time — wasting time and getting inconsistent results.
instructions: A Skill is a document with a fixed structure. Minimum contents: name (what the skill does), input (what must be provided), instruction (step-by-step direction to Claude), output (what Claude will return and in what format), example (a concrete input/output pair).
Choose a repeating operation from your work: summarising feedback, preparing a meeting agenda, analysing a competitor, a first-draft email. The more specific the better.

Write the SKILL.md: start with the name and one phrase explaining why this skill is needed. Then an Input section with a concrete example. Then Instructions — what Claude should do, step by step. Then Output — the exact result format. Finally, an example.
Test the skill: open Claude, paste the skill instruction as the system context, provide a test input and evaluate the output. Does it match the described format?
Iterate the skill until the output is stable across three different test inputs. Only then is the skill ready for use in a workflow.
wa-3.tip: The best first skill is one you already do manually every week. Do not invent new tasks to automate — formalise existing ones.
wa-3.validate: You have a finished SKILL.md that you have tested on at least two real inputs and received a predictable output.

wa-4.title: Chains: output of one step becomes input of the next
wa-4.why: Connecting steps into a chain is what turns a set of separate Claude interactions into a real workflow.
instructions: Chain principle: the final output of step N exactly matches the described input format of step N+1. If the formats do not match, a transformation step is needed between them.

Practice: take two skills you want to connect. Write down the output format of the first and the input format of the second. Is there a gap? Usually there is — the output is too verbose, or structured differently.

Three ways to close the gap: (1) add an explicit output format to the first skill's instruction that suits the next step, (2) create an intermediate transformer skill that converts the format, (3) add a human step — you manually edit the handoff.
Document the chain: draw a diagram where each block is one step, arrows show data transfer, and diamonds mark human review points. This diagram becomes the workflow documentation.
Test the entire chain end-to-end, not just individual steps. Errors most often appear at the seams between steps, not inside them.
wa-4.tip: Use explicit separators in prompts: 'Here is the output from the previous step: [DATA]. Now perform...'. Explicit context passing is more reliable than implicit.
wa-4.validate: You have connected at least two steps into a chain and run real data through it. The output of the second step matches the expected format.

wa-5.title: Quality control: human-in-the-loop and validate blocks
wa-5.why: Claude can make mistakes, hallucinate and interpret ambiguously — blind trust in output in a multi-step workflow leads to cascading errors.
instructions: Human-in-the-loop means points in the workflow where a human checks the result before passing it forward. You do not need to check every step — identify critical points where an error has the greatest consequences.

A validate block is an explicit criterion you check: 'the output contains exactly 5 items', 'all company names match the source data', 'the tone is formal, no jargon'. Write validate blocks for each step where this matters.

Three levels of control: (1) automatic — Claude checks against a checklist built into the instruction, (2) quick scan — 30 seconds, you look at structure and key data, (3) deep review — you read fully and compare with the source.
Red flags requiring deep review: specific numbers and statistics, names and titles, legal and financial language, quotes attributed to specific people.

Add a validate block directly to the skill instruction: 'At the end of your response add a checklist where you mark compliance with each of these criteria: [list]. If a criterion is not met, explain why'.
wa-5.tip: The best validate block is specific and binary: met / not met. 'The text sounds professional' is a bad criterion. 'Does not contain words from this list' is a good one.
wa-5.validate: Every step of your workflow has at least one explicit validate criterion and you know who (human or Claude) checks it.

wa-6.title: Scaling: document and hand off the workflow to your team
wa-6.why: A workflow that lives only in one person's head is not a scalable process — it is a personal habit. Documentation turns it into a team standard.
instructions: Workflow documentation structure: (1) name and purpose in one phrase, (2) when to use it — the trigger, (3) what to prepare — input data, (4) steps with links to Skills, (5) what a good result looks like, (6) common mistakes and how to avoid them.
Validate the documentation: ask a colleague who has never seen this workflow to read the document and try to run it independently. Where they get stuck — those are the gaps.
Versioning: add a 'last updated' date and a brief changelog. Workflows change — the team needs to know which version is current.
Storage: a Claude Project with instructions is ideal for storing workflow documents. All team members have access and the context is always current.
Improvement cycle: after every 10 workflow runs, hold a 15-minute retrospective. What worked? What took extra time? What gave unexpected results? Update the documentation.
wa-6.tip: Good workflow documentation is not a user manual — it is a work instruction. Write it as if you are explaining to a smart new employee who has never done this task.
wa-6.validate: You have a workflow document that another person can use without your verbal explanations. You have verified this in practice.

workflow-automation.trigger: A 3+ step routine repeats ≥3 times per week and eats your focus time.
inputs: Description of the current manual process
outputs: A workflow map: trigger → steps → outcome
A ready prompt + Project for the task
A before/after metric for the team report

claude-workspace.title: Claude's Workspace: Desktop and web from scratch
claude-workspace.subtitle: Three modes, every menu, and Settings — a walkthrough of each item
claude-workspace.whatItIs: A complete walkthrough of the Claude app (Desktop for macOS/Windows and web at [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]): three tabs — Chat, [[node:pl-cowork|Cowork]], and Code — plus the entire Settings screen. After this tutorial you understand what every menu does and can set up your workspace for projects and code deliberately instead of by guesswork.
claude-workspace.approach: We go top to bottom: install → the three modes → working in each → panels and shortcuts → Computer use → a full walkthrough of Settings (General, Account, Privacy, Billing, Usage, Capabilities, Connectors, Claude Code, Cowork) and the Desktop app section (General, Extensions, Developer) → the link with the CLI and troubleshooting.
outcomes: You understand the difference between the three modes — Chat / Cowork / Code — and when to use each
You know the purpose of every Settings item, not just General
You can pick the right permission mode (Ask / Auto accept / Plan / Auto / Bypass) for the task
You connect Connectors (MCP) and Desktop extensions safely
You set up Computer use with a clear understanding of its access boundaries and risks

applyIn.title: Starting work on code
applyIn.description: The Code tab: a session with Git isolation, project folder selection, permission mode, preview, and diff review.

applyIn.title: Long-running and background tasks
applyIn.description: Cowork and remote sessions: launch tasks that keep running even when the app is closed.

applyIn.title: Team onboarding
applyIn.description: A single walkthrough of Settings so colleagues don't get lost in the menus or run into limits.

pitfalls: Thinking Desktop is "just a chat": in reality it's three distinct modes with different capabilities.
Turning on Bypass permissions outside a sandbox — Claude runs commands without confirmation.
Ignoring Settings → Privacy and Capabilities — that's where both your data privacy and the available tools live.
Confusing local and remote sessions: a remote session has no @-files and no access to your local disk.
Enabling Computer use without understanding the app access tiers and the risk of prompt injection from the screen.

exercises.question: Open Chat, Cowork, and Code in turn. Note how the left menu differs in each mode.
exercises.hint: Chat — list of conversations; Cowork — tasks/schedules; Code — sessions.

exercises.question: Go through every Settings section and answer in one sentence: “why do I need it”.
exercises.hint: If you can’t answer, open it and read the caption.

exercises.question: Start your first local Code session in a test folder using Plan mode and review the plan without edits.
exercises.hint: Plan mode explores and proposes a plan without changing source files.

ws-1.title: Install and first sign-in
ws-1.why: Desktop gives you what the browser can't: parallel sessions, local files, a terminal, and extensions. But it has requirements.
instructions: Download the app: claude.com/download (macOS — universal, Windows — x64 or ARM64). Linux isn't supported — use the CLI there.
Launch it and sign in. For the Code tab on Windows you need Git for Windows — install it and restart the app.
The web version ([[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]) runs in the browser with no install, but without local files, a terminal, or the Desktop app section.
You can see the app version in the menu: macOS — Claude → About Claude; Windows — Help → About.
ws-1.validate: The app opened, you're signed in, and three tabs are visible at the top: Chat, Cowork, Code.
ws-1.tip: Desktop and the CLI can live side by side on one machine and even on the same project — they share the same config (CLAUDE.md, MCP).

ws-2.title: Three modes: Chat / Cowork / Code
ws-2.why: This is the app's main fork. Pick the wrong mode and you won't find the features you need.
instructions: Chat — a regular conversation: questions, text, working through files. The left menu is the list of conversations.
Cowork — agentic and long-running tasks: New task, Projects, Scheduled, Live artifacts, Dispatch (from your phone), Customize.
Code — development: each conversation is a "session" with its own history, project folder, and code changes; the menu has New session, Routines, Customize.
Rule of thumb: ask / write / work through something → Chat; hand off something long-running or scheduled → Cowork; code in a repository → Code.
ws-2.validate: You can explain in one sentence what each of the three tabs is for.
ws-2.tip: You can switch modes at the top at any time — no data is lost, and each mode keeps its own list on the left.

ws-3.title: Chat mode: the composer and the "+"
ws-3.why: This is where 80% of everyday work happens. The composer hides more than it looks.
instructions: Input field: type text + Enter. Next to it — the model picker (e.g. Opus/Sonnet) and the voice button (microphone).
The "+" button to the left of the field: attach files, connect [[node:skills|Skills]], [[node:mcp|Connectors]], and plugins.
You can change the model and the effort right inside a conversation — this affects reasoning depth and usage.
Drag files straight into the field — Claude will work through images and PDFs ([[node:cap-input-modalities|file and image support]]).
ws-3.validate: You found the model switcher and the "+" button and understand what each item behind them does.
ws-3.tip: Voice and response style are configured more deeply in Settings → General (Voice) — more on that below.

ws-4.title: Cowork mode: tasks, schedules, Dispatch
ws-4.why: Cowork is Claude working on its own and over long stretches — including while you're away from the computer.
instructions: New task — set up a task; "Work in a project" ties it to a [[node:projects|project]] with its knowledge and instructions.
Scheduled — recurring tasks on a schedule (for example, a daily digest).
Live artifacts — result artifacts that keep updating; Dispatch (Beta) — sending tasks to Claude from your phone.
Customize — manage connectors, skills, and plugins in one place.
A detailed walkthrough of Cowork is in a separate tutorial: [[tutorial:claude-cowork|Claude Cowork]].
ws-4.validate: You understand how New task differs from Scheduled and what Dispatch is.
ws-4.tip: Dispatch and schedules require a Pro or Max plan and don't work on Team/Enterprise.

ws-5.title: Code mode: starting a session
ws-5.why: Before your first message in Code you need to set four things — otherwise Claude will start in the wrong place and the wrong way.
instructions: Environment — where it runs: Local (your machine), Remote (Anthropic's cloud, keeps going when the app is closed), SSH (your own server).
Project folder — the folder or repository Claude works with. For Remote you can add several repositories.
Model — the model picker next to the send button; change it as you go.
Permission mode — how much freedom Claude has (the next step). Enter your task and hit Enter.
ws-5.validate: Before sending, you can see the Environment, folder, model, and permission mode pickers.
ws-5.tip: For long refactors and test runs, choose Remote — the task won't be interrupted even if you close the app.

ws-6.title: Permission modes
ws-6.why: This is the main safeguard: it decides whether Claude asks before changing files and running commands.
instructions: Ask permissions (default) — asks before every edit/command and shows a diff. Recommended for beginners.
Auto accept edits — accepts file edits and safe commands (mkdir, mv) on its own, but asks about other commands.
Plan mode — explores and proposes a plan without touching the source. Great for complex "think first" tasks.
Auto — does everything with background safety checks (research preview, requires a recent Opus/Sonnet).
Bypass permissions — no confirmations at all. Sandbox/VM only; enabled in Settings → Claude Code.
ws-6.validate: You can pick the right mode for a task and know which one is dangerous outside a sandbox.
ws-6.tip: A solid workflow: start in Plan → approve the plan → switch to Auto accept edits to carry it out.

ws-7.title: Working with code: context and control
ws-7.why: The sharper the context and the better you steer Claude, the less rework you get.
instructions: @-mention a file: type @ and the name — the file goes into context (not available in Remote).
Attachments: images, PDFs, screenshots of bugs — via the button or by dragging them in.
Interrupting: the stop button halts immediately; or just type a correction and hit Enter — Claude will factor it in after the current step.
Claude reads the project files, makes edits, and runs commands according to the permission mode you chose.
ws-7.validate: You added a file via @ and steered Claude with a correction without stopping its work.
ws-7.tip: A short clarifying correction mid-run is cheaper than fully restarting the task.

ws-8.title: Preview, diff, and code review
ws-8.why: Desktop shows changes visually and checks them itself — this removes "blind" edits.
instructions: Preview — Claude spins up a dev server and opens a built-in browser; auto-verification takes screenshots and clicks elements after edits.
Diff: an indicator like "+12 −1" opens the per-file change view; click a line to leave a comment.
Submit comments: macOS — Cmd+Enter, Windows — Ctrl+Enter; Claude makes the edits and shows a new diff.
"Review code" in the diff view — Claude looks for bugs, logic issues, and security problems on its own (not style).
After a PR, a CI panel appears: Auto-fix and Auto-merge toggles.
ws-8.validate: You opened a diff, left a comment, and requested "Review code".
ws-8.tip: The preview server config lives in .claude/launch.json — that's where you put your own launch command and port.

ws-9.title: The workspace: panels and shortcuts
ws-9.why: Code is built from panels you arrange to suit yourself — this speeds up your work enormously.
instructions: Panels: chat, diff, preview, terminal, file, plan, tasks, subagent. Open them from the Views menu and drag them by the title.
Terminal: Ctrl+` — opens in the session folder, the same environment Claude uses (npm test, git status).
Files: click a path to open the file; make targeted edits + Save.
Transcript modes (Normal/Verbose/Summary) — Ctrl+O. All shortcuts — Cmd+/ (macOS) or Ctrl+/ (Windows).
ws-9.validate: You opened a second panel from Views and switched the transcript mode.
ws-9.tip: Verbose shows every step Claude takes — handy when you need to understand why it did something a certain way.

ws-10.title: Parallel sessions and isolation
ws-10.why: You can run several tasks at once without worrying they'll get mixed up.
instructions: + New session (Cmd+N) — a new parallel session; Ctrl+Tab switches between them.
For Git repositories, each session gets its own isolated copy via a worktree — edits don't overlap until a commit.
Side-chat (Cmd+; or /btw) — an aside question with the session's context, without cluttering the main conversation.
The Tasks panel shows background work: subagents and background commands.
ws-10.validate: You opened two sessions and understand why their edits don't conflict.
ws-10.tip: Auto-archive after a merge/closed PR (Settings → Claude Code) clears out finished sessions for you.

ws-11.title: Computer use: screen control
ws-11.why: Claude can control apps on your screen — powerful, but it requires deliberate boundaries.
instructions: Enabled in Settings → General (Desktop app section) with the Computer use toggle. On macOS it needs Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions.
Requires a Pro or Max plan (not Team/Enterprise) and a running Desktop app.
Access tiers are fixed: browsers — view only, terminals/IDEs — clicks only, everything else — full control.
More on safe, isolated execution — [[node:sys-agent-sandbox|an isolated environment for the agent]] and [[node:cap-computer|Computer use]].
ws-11.validate: You understand which permissions are needed and why a browser is "view only".
ws-11.tip: Claude flags suspicious on-screen text as possible prompt injection, but the trust boundary here is different — don't run it on sensitive data.

ws-12.title: Settings — part 1: General and Account
ws-12.why: General sets how Claude addresses you and behaves everywhere; Account is about devices and sign-in security.
instructions: General → Profile: name, "what to call you", occupation, and Instructions for Claude — general guidance for all chats and Cowork ([[node:i-global|global instructions]]).
General → Preferences: Appearance (system/light/dark), Chat font.
General → Voice (voice style and speed) and Notifications (response completion, Code notifications, permission requests, Dispatch messages).
Account: "Log out of all devices", Organization ID, the list of active sessions (device, city, dates), account deletion.
ws-12.validate: You filled in Instructions for Claude and found the list of active sessions in Account.
ws-12.tip: Instructions for Claude is the most underrated item: one setting improves the tone and format across all your future conversations.

ws-13.title: Settings — part 2: Privacy, Billing, Usage, Capabilities
ws-13.why: This is where data privacy, money, and which tools Claude can use at all live.
instructions: Privacy — how your data is used and model training; go through this section deliberately ([[node:pl-privacy|privacy]]).
Billing — plan and payment; Usage — usage by period and by model (the plan is shared across all Claude surfaces).
Capabilities — toggles for Claude's capabilities (web search, analysis, and so on).
The usage ring next to the model picker in Code shows the session context and the plan's overall usage.
ws-13.validate: You know where to check usage and where to turn capabilities on and off.
ws-13.tip: If you're hitting limits — check Usage first and compare models before upgrading your plan.

ws-14.title: Settings — part 3: Connectors, Claude Code, Cowork
ws-14.why: These are the app's "sockets": external services, the behavior of code sessions, and agentic-mode settings.
instructions: Connectors — integrations (Google Calendar, Slack, GitHub, Linear, Notion …). These are [[node:mcp|MCP servers]] with a graphical setup; they can also be added from the "+" in the composer.
For services not on the list — add MCP manually via the config files; custom connectors exist too.
Claude Code — the behavior of Code sessions: allow Bypass permissions, worktree location, auto-archive after a PR, turning Preview and Persist sessions on/off.
Cowork — agentic-mode and Dispatch settings.
ws-14.validate: You opened Connectors and understand that these are MCP with a convenient connection wizard.
ws-14.tip: Disconnect/Manage connectors — right there in Settings → Connectors, or via "Manage connectors" in the composer.

ws-15.title: The Desktop app section: General, Extensions, Developer
ws-15.why: This is what the browser doesn't have: local extensions and connecting your own MCP servers.
instructions: Desktop app → General: the Computer use toggle, the status of system permissions, Denied apps (apps Claude won't touch), and "Unhide apps when Claude finishes".
Extensions — install extensions/connectors in one click, no terminal needed.
Developer — connect local MCP servers and developer configuration.
MCP from the chat app (claude_desktop_config.json) is picked up in the Code tab too.
ws-15.validate: You found the Computer use toggle in Desktop app → General and understand what Developer is for.
ws-15.tip: If an MCP server isn't responding on Windows — check the config, restart the app, and see whether the server process is still alive in Task Manager.

ws-16.title: CLI ↔ Desktop and troubleshooting
ws-16.why: Desktop and the [[node:claude-code|CLI]] are one engine; knowing the link, you don't lose settings and you fix issues fast.
instructions: Shared config: CLAUDE.md, MCP servers (~/.claude.json, .mcp.json), hooks, skills, settings — all work in both.
Move a session from the terminal to Desktop: the /desktop command (when signed in with a subscription).
What Desktop lacks: third-party providers (Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry), Linux, inline suggestions, agent teams, terminal dialogs (/permissions, /config, /agents).
Troubleshooting: 403 — sign out and back in; blank screen — restart/update; on Windows, Code needs Git.
ws-16.validate: You understand that the config is shared and know the first thing to do on a 403 error.
ws-16.tip: Use Desktop for parallel sessions and visual review, and the CLI for scripts and automation.

project-files.title: Uploading files to a Project
project-files.subtitle: How to give Claude documents as context and ask questions about them
project-files.whatItIs: A walkthrough of how to upload files to a [[node:projects|Project]] so Claude answers based on your documents — brand guidelines, specs, code, spreadsheets — instead of relying on general knowledge.
project-files.approach: We move from "what Claude can read" → how and where to upload → what belongs in project knowledge versus a chat → how to phrase a request about the files → common mistakes → keeping everything current.
outcomes: Understand which formats Claude can read and how it uses them in its answers
Know the difference between project knowledge and an attachment in a single chat
Can reference a file in your request and get an answer based strictly on it
Avoid duplicates and outdated files that spoil the answers

applyIn.title: Working from a brand guide
applyIn.description: Upload the guide to a Project, and every piece of text is written in your tone of voice.

applyIn.title: Document analysis
applyIn.description: PDF contracts, reports, specs: ask about the contents without copying the text by hand.

applyIn.title: Context for code
applyIn.description: Upload the key files or the schema, and Claude answers with your project in mind.

pitfalls: Dropping a file into a single chat when it's needed across every conversation in the project — it belongs in the Project's knowledge.
Keeping outdated versions of files: Claude will trust the old document.
Uploading dozens of files "just in case" — the extra context dilutes the answer.
Asking about a file without naming it when there are many — specify exactly which one.

exercises.question: Create a Project, upload a single document into its knowledge (for example, a brand guide), and ask a question that can only be answered from that file.
exercises.hint: If Claude answers in general terms, check that the file is in the Project's knowledge, not just attached to a chat.

exercises.question: Compare: ask the same question with the file uploaded and without it. What changed in the answer?
exercises.hint: That difference is exactly the value of context from the file.

pf-1.title: What Claude can read
pf-1.why: Before you upload anything, understand which files are actually useful and how Claude "sees" them.
instructions: Supported formats include PDF, DOCX, text, code, spreadsheets (CSV/XLSX), and images ([[node:cap-input-modalities|file and image support]]).
Claude reads the contents as part of the context: it quotes, summarizes, and answers based on them.
It can also parse images and scans (Vision), but the quality depends on how legible they are.
Large files take up context — this affects how long the conversation can run; don't upload more than you need.
pf-1.validate: You understand which formats to upload and what Claude does with them.
pf-1.tip: If the document is a table of numbers, first ask Claude to restate its structure so you can confirm it read it correctly.

pf-2.title: How and where to upload
pf-2.why: There are two places for files, and your choice determines which conversations Claude will see them in.
instructions: Project knowledge: open the [[node:projects|Project]] → the knowledge/files section → add the document. It's available across every conversation in that project.
Chat attachment: use the attach button or drag the file straight into the input field — the file only lives in that one conversation.
Rule of thumb: permanent and shared → Project knowledge; one-off → chat attachment.
You can drag files in with the mouse, and several at once too.
pf-2.validate: You've added a file to the Project's knowledge and understand how that differs from a chat attachment.
pf-2.tip: If you need the same file again and again, it definitely belongs in the Project's knowledge rather than in each new chat.

pf-3.title: What goes into knowledge versus into a chat
pf-3.why: Project knowledge is the "permanent memory." The stable things go there; the variable things go into a chat.
instructions: Into Project knowledge: brand guide, tone of voice, specs, templates, reference materials — whatever you need all the time.
Into a chat: a one-off document for a specific task (a single contract, one report to review).
The link to [[node:p-instructions|project instructions]]: files are the "what to know," instructions are the "how to behave."
Don't mix them: a dozen one-off files in the knowledge becomes clutter that gets in the way.
pf-3.validate: For any given file, you can decide whether it's permanent (into knowledge) or one-off (into a chat).
pf-3.tip: Set yourself a rule: Project knowledge = only the things that will outlive the current task.

pf-4.title: How to ask about a file
pf-4.why: The file is uploaded — now you need to reference it correctly so the answer stays strictly within the document.
instructions: Name the source: "using the brand guide, write a post…", "based on section 3 of the contract, answer…".
If there are many files, specify exactly which one to answer from.
Ask for verifiability: "quote the passage your answer is based on."
Example: upload the brand guide and ask, "write a 3-paragraph announcement in our tone of voice."
pf-4.validate: You got an answer that clearly draws on the uploaded file rather than on general knowledge.
pf-4.tip: Asking "quote where you got this" quickly reveals whether Claude actually read the file or just made it up.

pf-5.title: Common mistakes
pf-5.why: Most cases of "Claude gives the wrong answer" about files come down to four typical mistakes.
instructions: Outdated file: an old version is sitting there and Claude trusts it. Keep a single current one.
Duplicates: two versions of the same document confuse the model. Delete the extra one.
Overload: dozens of files blur the focus. Keep only what the task needs.
Wrong container: a file attached to a chat isn't visible in the project's other conversations.
pf-5.validate: You recognize these four mistakes and know how to fix each one.
pf-5.tip: If an answer seems off, first check which file is actually uploaded and whether it's out of date.

pf-6.title: Keeping things current
pf-6.why: Files go stale. Project knowledge is only as useful as it is fresh.
instructions: Periodically review the Project's knowledge: replace what's outdated, remove what's unnecessary.
When a document changes substantially, upload the new version and delete the old one.
Keep a "single source of truth": one current file per topic.
Next, set up your [[node:p-instructions|project instructions]] so Claude knows how to use these files.
pf-6.validate: The Project's knowledge holds only current files, one per topic.
pf-6.tip: Tie this to a regular cleanup: an outdated brand guide is worse than no brand guide at all.
